Thank you. Decent youth jobs. infrastructure development, and continuous policy reforms. Allow me to highlight recent economic improvements aimed at accelerating the implementation of the SDGs in Lesotho. Lesotho's economy is growing moderately and at an average of 2% of GDP per annum. Domestic revenue as a share of GDP has improved. Domestic tax contributions remain below the 25% benchmark, The Southern African Customs Union transfers continue to dominate revenue while remittances are stable, averaging over 20% of GDP. Secondly, digital access has expanded via mobile platforms with internet usage having risen to 48%. Financial inclusion has improved with 80% of adults having access to financial services in 2021. Due to a surge in mobile money uptake. The use of mobile money has become prevalent among MSMEs for payments and business transactions. Thirdly, our universal healthcare service coverage index of 53% shows moderate access to essential health services. Household contribution to the health sector is 1% of healthcare spending, attributed to the abolishment of user fees at primary healthcare level, with highly subsidized fees at primary and tertiary healthcare levels. 4, Lesotho has taken important steps to advance gender equality. Women's political participation has improved at local and national government levels, while representation in national leadership and managerial positions remain low. Progress was recorded in women's autonomy in reproductive decision-making. Overall, early marriage has declined marginally, but rates remain high in rural and underprivileged communities. Gender-based violence remains a significant challenge. Number 5, climate change resilience improved through early warning systems and disaster risk financing. Core planning targets were achieved with the nationally determined contribution and national adaptation plan having been updated. Climate education has been mainstreamed into schools' curricula and creative awareness campaigns. These steps reflect a growing climate ambition. Despite Lesotho being landlocked, SDG 14 remains relevant. Lesotho relies on inland water bodies for livelihoods, biodiversity, and regional water security. Notable gains include a decline in nutrient pollution through organic farming and pesticide controls, while plastic waste is being addressed through fiscal tools and recycling initiatives. Sustainable fish stocks have been maintained, with Lesotho becoming Africa's top producer of rainbow trout. Economic benefits continue to grow in aquaculture and ecotourism. Number 6, openness in trade to enhance integration is vital for a landlocked country like ours. Our progress to date was achieved through strategic priorities such as the Africa Continental Free Trade Area integration, domestic resource mobilization, SDG localization, diaspora engagement, and disaster risk reduction. We advocate for a rules-based, free and open trade system that promotes integration and mutual benefits. We are determined to accelerate progress by mainstreaming SDGs into national planning and budgets and budgeting processes, aligning our operational plans with the Pact for the Future and implementing reforms to strengthen domestic financial resources. Our progress has been underpinned by key strategic interventions, including integration into the Africa Continental Free Trade Area, strengthened domestic resource mobilization, localization of the Sustainable Development Goals, engagement of the diaspora, and robust disaster risk framework. Lesotho remains resolute in its commitment to achieving 2030 Agenda for the SDGs. The government is actively mainstreaming the SDGs into national planning and budgeting frameworks. Operational plans are being aligned with the United Nations Pact for the Future, and structural reforms are underway to enhance domestic financial resource mobilization. We thank the global community for supporting us as we strive to deliver a just, inclusive, and sustainable future for all. To conclude, we appeal to our development partners to live up to the commitments made during the SDG Summit in 2023, in the Pact for the Future, and recently held FFD4 conference in Sevilla, to super and turbocharge the implementation of SDGs, especially in developing countries like the Kingdom of Lesotho. Thank you, Mr. President.

Next, increasing investment in human resources development, including quality education systems, to better prevent, prepare, and respond to future pandemics, emerging challenges, and future shocks. Scaling up cooperation in disaster risk reduction and addressing climate change, and other environmental issues to support the achievement of a resilient ASEAN community. We envision a future-ready economy for our region anchored on sustainable growth and good governance, which will promote inclusive, participatory, and equitable access to economic opportunities. And its mutually reinforcing nature with regionalization— regionalism by solidifying adherence to the principles of the UN Charter. And now, Mr. Vice President, in my national capacity, I wish to deliver the following statement. We recognize the UN as a vital catalyst for change, amplifying partnerships, driving innovation, and supporting member states to build resilient, inclusive, and sustainable societies. Guided by our Whole-of-Nation-Plus approach, the Philippines continues to catalyze transformative change for sustainable development through evidence-based policymaking, inclusive economic strategies, and targeted social investments, ensuring that we identify those that are at risk of being left behind and reaching those who are farthest behind first. We are increasing investments in human capital development, enhancing access to education, healthcare, nutrition, and early childhood care and development to break the cycle of intergenerational poverty. We crafted the Trabaho Para sa Bayan Plan, which is a comprehensive National Employment Master Plan to future-proof our labor market and enhance labor market governance in recognition of the fast-changing world of work. We also enacted the Philippine Ecosystem Natural Capital Accounting Act, to mainstream environmental and ecosystem valuation into national planning and policymaking, reinforcing a capacity for sustainable data-driven decisions. With just 5 years remaining, and as we confront complex global challenges, we recognize the interconnected nature of the SDGs and the need for a global response tailored to the circumstances and priorities of countries, including middle-income countries. The Philippines calls for renewed solidarity in advancing the 2030 Agenda and making good on the promise of a sustainable, just, and resilient future for all. Thank you very much.

Evidence shows that the economic cost of not investing in justice, estimated at up to 3% of GDP, is often far greater than the cost of delivering it. Unresolved legal problems drive poverty and inequality. They spark unrest, erode trust in institutions, and undermine social cohesion. We need a systemic approach that centers human rights and anticipates risks before they escalate. An evidence-based approach that focuses on how individuals experience justice processes to improve their justice journeys. This approach requires justice institutions to collaborate with a wide range of actors, including those beyond the formal justice sector or the justice sector at all. But to truly deliver justice and overcome the global gap of 5.1 billion people without equal access to justice, we must address the inequities that persist globally. Gender equality is limiting women's ability to resolve legal problems, leading to negative outcomes including violence, financial hardship, and discrimination. Additionally, children and adolescents continue to be systematically excluded from the benefits of justice. It is imperative to highlight the increased risks experienced by women and children involved in the same case, especially in situations of violence within family contexts, resulting in compounded justice problems. Thus, justice systems must be built with services that are safe, affordable, and designed with women's and children's needs in mind. Structural transformation of justice systems must include institutional redesign. We must also recognize the hindered access to justice experienced by persons with disabilities. They make up about 16% of the world's population, and they are continuously left behind. We call for people-centered justice systems that will ensure accommodations, accessible communication formats, legal aid, and meaningful participation of persons with disabilities to reduce obstacles and advance individual rights and social inclusion. Mr. President, delivering on the promise to leave no one behind means using justice as the key to achieving equal, inclusive, and sustainable development. It means ensuring that those most often excluded, including women and children, Thank you. We need to ensure that all people can access justice when they need it and how they need it. To achieve this, we must move from rhetoric to investment. Investing in justice is investing in prevention, in peace, and in the resilience of our societies. It is a smart, cost-effective investment with long-term returns, both human and economic. Mr. President, as members of the Justice Action Coalition, we call on all partners to prioritize equal access to justice for all. Let us commit today and every day to ensuring that justice is not an afterthought but a foundation. Thank you.

I thank His Excellency Minister Madeira, spoke on behalf of the Justice Action Coalition, and I understand you got this delivering this statement on behalf of your own country. The Dominican Republic. Okay, the floor is yours again.

Muchas gracias.
I thank His Excellency Minister Madera, and now I give the floor to Her Excellency Fatou Kinteh, the Minister of Gender, Children and Social Welfare of Gambia.

On behalf of the Group of 77 and China, this year's theme on advancing sustainable development, inclusive science and evidence-based solutions for the 2030 Agenda and its SDGs for leaving no one behind is both timely and urgent. For The Gambia, the theme reflects ongoing efforts in creating sustainability, inclusivity, and data-driven decision-making at the heart of our national development. Since adopting the 2030 Agenda, The Gambia has remained steadfast in its commitment to the SDGs, embedding them into our national strategies and development plans. Our recovery-focused National Development Plan 2023-2027 is built on the principle of inclusion, recognizing that social and economic resilience cannot be achieved unless all segments of society, especially women and children, are empowered and supported. Through evidence-based planning and inclusive governance, we have sought to ensure that national policies are responsive to real needs of our people. Our targeted national review during this forum is a testament to this commitment. It reflects not only the work undertaken across sectors, from health and social protection to youth empowerment and climate resilience, but also the broad participation of stakeholders at all levels. We use data, community engagement, and institutional coordination to drive progress where it matters most in the lives of all Gambians. Yet, Mr. President, challenges still remain. The path to 2030 is narrowing and progress is uneven. Globally, only 17% of the SDG targets are on track, and The Gambia is not immune to the constraints faced in many developing countries. Shrinking development assistance, rising debt servicing costs, and climate-induced shocks continue to pressure our limited resources and hamper long-term planning. Our economy remains vulnerable, heavily reliant on sectors sensitive to external shocks. High levels of informal employment, persistent gender disparities, and youth unemployment also present major barriers to inclusive growth. Mr. President, as we enter the final stretch of the decade of action, the urgency to deliver results has never been paramount— more paramount. The political will, though unwavering, is not enough. We need mobilization of adequate political and sustainable financial resources and targeted technical support to match our ambition. The Gambia strongly supports innovative solutions such as debt-for-development and debt-for-climate swaps, These mechanisms would offer countries like ours the opportunity to redirect resources away from debt servicing towards climate resilience, education, health, and poverty eradication. We also call for a more inclusive and equitable global financial architecture that recognizes the developmental needs of small, vulnerable communities and economies and enables long-term investment in sustainable development. In conclusion, the government remains firmly committed to the 2030 Agenda. We are strengthening national capacities to align public finance with development priorities, improving data systems to track and assess progress, and—

Thank you. Perfect timing. I, I thank Her Excellency Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Honduras, and now I give the floor to His Excellency Alan García Monterrosa, Undersecretary of Strategic Analysis for Development of Guatemala.

Mr. President, distinguished forum, I come from Guatemala, the heart of the Maya world, a multilingual, multiethnic land of volcanoes where very often Strength emerges from crisis. Today, my country is at a critical juncture, a democratic transformation born out of a fundamental principle. So as to not fly blind, democracy has to listen, and we have indeed listened. These are victories that give us hope. But as you— as we know, averages hide individual histories. The real history of our labor market is one of informality. The real story of our health is that of an immense gulf between urban centers and rural communities where universal access One that we want to offer to the international— the multilateral system at its 80th anniversary, and that is that global challenges cannot be addressed with solutions that leave half of the people out. I thank His Excellency Minister García Monterrosa of Guatemala, and now I give the floor to His Excellency Domagoj Mikulić, State Secretary, Ministry of Regional Development, EU Funds of Croatia.

Our journey from the recovery after the Homeland War to the current role as a constructive and reliable member of the UN, NATO, and the EU has been shaped by resilience, reform, and dedication to peace, security, and sustainable development. Recovery has brought political stability, economic growth, and global engagement, reflected today also in readiness to join the OECD. And in this context, catalyzing change is not a choice; it is a necessity. Our experiences reinforce our conviction that revitalized and reformed United Nations is essential to effectively address the evolving global challenges of today and tomorrow. Croatia is fully committed to the 2030 Agenda, its efficient and timely implementation. It serves as our strategic compass for our national development, closely aligned with our National Development Strategy. We have embedded sustainability into our policies, financial frameworks, and local development, ranking 8th among 193 UN countries in implementing the Sustainable Development Goals while maintaining the 3.6% GDP growth. In recent years, we have made significant progress in decentralizing sustainable development efforts and strengthening the capacity of subnational authorities. However, in parallel, we recognize that further efforts are essential for catalyzing meaningful and lasting change. So at the end, allow me to convey our main message: the Republic of Croatia remains a reliable and constructive partner in advancing the 2030 Agenda and in shaping a more peaceful, just and sustainable future for all. Thank you.

I thank His Excellency Minister Mikulić of Croatia. And now I give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Markus Roibi, State Secretary, Delegate of the Federal Council for the 2030 Agenda of Switzerland. Switzerland.

I thank Her Excellency Minister Granados Galvano of Spain. And now I give the floor to His Excellency Assan Darbayev, Vice Minister of National Economy of the Republic of Kazakhstan.

Mr. Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, it is a pleasure to present the 3rd Voluntary National Review on behalf of Kazakhstan. Sustainability principles are integrated into the state planning system, including the National Development Plan until 2029, and cover, cover a wide range of social, economical, and environmental priorities. Russia, for its part, is accelerating progress toward the achievement of current goals. On July 24th, an independent report on Russia's progress was presented on the sidelines of the forum. The key conclusion of the report is that we are confidently moving forward. Russia shows progress on 61% of SDG indicators. Poverty has been reduced by more 1.5 times. Women hold 48.8% of leadership positions, and the share of low-carbon energy generation, including gas and nuclear, has reached 87%. I particularly want to highlight successes under SDG 8. The economy grew by more than 4% annually during 2023-2024, and unemployment fell to 2.3% by the end of 2024. A particularly important contribution to economic growth came from the small and medium business sector. Tax revenues nearly doubled in this area, reaching $119 billion. This was made possible by digital super services, platforms that integrate registration, banking, and fiscal services that allowed to bring small businesses out of the gray economy. These platforms can operate not only in Russia, they can be make a significant contribution to mobilizing domestic resources in other countries. For example, in Kyrgyzstan, their implementation has allowed for a doubling of the SME tax base. Russia's proposed solutions are sustainable and inclusive. They embody the principles of fair, mutually beneficial cooperation based on the UN Charter. We are convinced that adhering to these principles will reduce conflict and help sustainable development. Unfortunately, we are also facing neocolonial practices, restrictions on access to technologies, markets, and resources. This contradicts the spirit of cooperation. In conclusion, I'd like to highlight that Russia is maintaining its international development assistance at $1 billion per year and actively participates in regional and global initiatives through the EAEU, BRICS, SCO, G20, and the UN. Thank you for your attention. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank His Excellency, Representative of the Russian Federation, and now I give the floor to His Excellency Bereket Tesfamariam, Minister of Planning and Development of Ethiopia.

Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. This year's theme of the Forum could not have come at a more propitious time, given the growing importance of employing science and evidence-based solutions to accelerate the implementation of the SDGs. The SDGs selected for this year's review offer a chance to share experience and best practices for advancing implementation. Ethiopia has made notable progress on many goals, and as we present our voluntary national review, I wish to highlight key achievements on the goals under this year's forum. With regard to ensuring healthy lives, and promote well-being for all, maternal mortality ratio has dropped significantly. Similar gains have also been achieved in reducing under-5 mortality, with every child now, regardless of location, is counted, tracked, and protected from preventable disease. Ethiopia is therefore on track with some of the targets, still need intervention in areas of neonatal mortality and coverage of essential services. Gender equality remains a strategic pillar of our national development agenda, and thus we have not fallen short in our commitment to address the challenge surrounding SDG 5. In the same vein, as one of the fastest growing economies in Africa and with an increasing youth population, enormous amount of effort has been made to ensure sustained and inclusive economic growth, full and productive employment through the implementation of our homegrown economic reform. This is one area in which our success is largely attributed to the resilient and reform-driven economy. Furthermore, Ethiopia Green Legacy Initiative and National Wheat Program are contributing significantly to food security, preserving biodiversity, and improving the livelihood of rural communities through harnessing our rich and diverse inland freshwater bodies. Mr. President, in accelerating implementation of the SDGs, Ethiopia underscores that partnership and international cooperation still remain critical variables in the overall achievement of the goals. In this regard, strengthening North-South and South-South cooperation, availing development financing, and providing support through capacity building are all paramount to the realization of SDGs. In conclusion, Mr. President, while I reiterate the firm commitment of our government to work with all for the realization of Agenda 2030, I would like to seize this opportunity to extend our invitation to participate, to attend our Voluntary National Review, which will be held on 23rd July 2025. I hope to see you all there. Thank you.
Thank you. I thank very much His Excellency Minister Tesfaye Mariam of Ethiopia. And now I give the floor to His Excellency Boniface Barasa Makoka, Principal Secretary for Economic Planning of Kenya.

Thank you, Chair, Excellencies, distinguished guests. Kenya aligns with the statement of Group of 77 and China and wishes to add the following remarks in its national capacity. As the UN marks its 80th anniversary, Kenya extends its profound appreciation for the organization's enduring role in promoting peace, security, and global development. The 2025 High-Level Political Forum takes place at a critical juncture. With only 5 years to the 2030 deadline, progress on most targets of Sustainable Development Goals remains slow and insufficient. The ongoing presentation of voluntary National reviews evidently shows mixed results, with some SDGs targets progressing while others are either stagnating or regressing. It is therefore imperative to strengthen support to developing countries to enhance the means of implementation to accelerate the achievement of the SDGs. Chair. In July 2024, Kenya presented her 3rd voluntary national review, and our review indicated substantial progress on some targets, but overall progress remains slow. While Kenya remains committed to the SDG implementation, we stress that strong and inclusive development partnership and collaborative efforts supported by non-financial means of implementation including in technology transfer, data systems, and capacity building, remains essential for inclusive development globally. So adequate and affordable financing remains a challenge for most developing countries. Without affordable credit and open markets, development progress will stall. On 30th June 2025, world leaders gathered in Seville, Spain, for the 4th Financing for Development Conference and adopted the Seville Commitment. This renewed global framework provides hope and optimism to our collective efforts. Its full implementation is expected to add impetus to the achievement of SDGs, leaving no one behind. Kenya supports the call for reforms of international financial architecture in addressing systemic issues to unlock affordable and predictable financing for the SDGs. Further, we need a development-oriented sovereign debt architecture where public debt fosters progress and is not a recipe for distress. Finally, we call upon developed countries to honor their our longstanding commitments towards global development, including ODA commitments. Thank you.
I thank His Excellency, Minister of Kenya, and now I give the floor to His Excellency Ahmad Mbodou Mahamat, President of the Social, Economic, Environmental and Cultural Council of Chad.

President, ladies and gentlemen, National delegations, all protocols observed. Allow me at the outset to convey the warm fraternal greetings of the government, of people of Chad, whose hopes and dreams are the full implementation of the SDGs. Looking to the shortcomings of our current global system and our inability to find efficient solutions to global crises. This meeting presents an opportunity to reaffirm a commitment to the United Nations Charter, to revitalize multilateralism and respect for the recommendations of the 4th Financing for Development Conference in order to implement the SDGs and find innovative inclusive challenges for inclusive— for emerging challenges. Since September 2015, Chad has been working to effectively implement the SDGs. This has led to the preparation and presentation of 3 voluntary national reviews in 2019, 2021, and 2024. The government of Chad is committed to leaving no one behind and including the most vulnerable groups in its programs and analysis. We plan to hold financing roundtables in September in Dubai in order to find realistic solutions to the needs of our populations. In terms of peacebuilding, the government of Chad led by the vision of the President of the Republic and Head of State, Idriss Déby, has ensured a peaceful transition that has allowed to restore constitutional order in 2024. Today, we enjoy stability and host populations from neighboring countries that face various security crises. In terms of our environmental policy, despite our vulnerability to climate change and despite our adaptation efforts, our country has been unable to meet some of its goals in terms of climate change impacts. Ladies and gentlemen, developing countries such as Chad require increased international support in order to keep the necessary pace to achieve the SDGs by 2030. We have suffered from internal conflict and regional tensions, which have impacted our development process. However, we firmly believe that international cooperation and multilateral dialogue are key to overcoming these challenges. Thank you for your attention.
Thank you, Minister of Chad. And now I give the floor to Mr. Martin Alves. Director-General of the Cooperation of Uruguay.

Thank you, Mr. President, distinguished delegates. As we approach the 80th anniversary of the United Nations Charter, it's essential that we reiterate our collective commitment to the sustainable development pillar. The 2030 Agenda should not be seen as a promise that can be put off, but rather it must be reaffirmed as the roadmap for our efforts and our resources based on equity, solidarity, and human rights. For Uruguay, health, gender equality, decent work, the protection of the oceans, and international cooperation are not isolated spheres. Rather, they are interdependent dimensions that guarantee collective well-being. Being and the sustainability of the planet. We reaffirm the importance of having solid, universal, and equitable healthcare systems. Particularly, Uruguay has strengthened its mental health policy for the prevention of noncommunicable diseases, as well as universal access to sexual and reproductive health with a rights-based approach and primary care approach. These efforts have in particular focused on teenagers, women and girls, as well as vulnerable populations, including rural areas. Moreover, the effects of climate change are being incorporated into public health planning, recognizing their growing impact on this area. Gender equality is not a sectoral goal; rather, it is an essential condition for sustainable development. Uruguay has promoted the adaptation of care models. Recognizing the economic and social value of non-remunerated work and also redistributing responsibilities between the state, families, and the community. The national care system, monetary transfers to mitigate the effects of feminization and infantilization of poverty, as well as social dialogue spaces are all part of the strategy. However, we warn that without adequate financing, As a complement to international public financing. International cooperation should occupy a central role in times of growing fragmentation. Multilateralism must be defended in order to strengthen global and inter-regional partnerships. We hope that the political document of this forum will soon be adopted by consensus. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Uruguay. And now I give the floor to Her Excellency Ana Isabel Marques Xavier, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and Cooperation of Portugal.

Chair, Excellencies, let me begin with a clear message. on the 8th anniversary of the UN Charter. Portugal is fully committed to multilateralism and to the implementation of the 2030 Agenda and the Pact for the Future. This is the time to act together. To deliver a balanced reform of our UN towards a more effective organization. To deliver on our commitments with greater coherence, urgency, and ambition. It is our shared responsibility. Portugal is doing its part. First, following up on our second Voluntary National Review in 2023, we are finalizing a national roadmap to strengthen policy coherence for sustainable development across sectors, across government and across our international cooperation. For more comprehensive work and results in the future, also building on the increasing number of voluntary local reviews presented by Portuguese municipalities, this year 4 joined: Almada, Fundão, Grândola, and Odmira. Second, We continue to invest in international partnerships for the SDGs, especially in countries in more vulnerable situations. That is why we have developed 3 fellowships with the United Nations for developing countries, focusing on capacity building on the ocean, digital transformation, and outer space. Thirdly and finally, Looking to the SDGs under review this year, and as noted throughout the past week by our delegation, allow me to highlight our strong support to the implementation of the UNOC3 Political Declaration and the Compromiso de Sevilla as key roadmaps for the advancement of SDG 14 and SDG 17, from the MVI to the BBNP. And the promotion of debt-for-nature swaps and triangular cooperation, among others. Also, our commitment to the success of the World Social Summit as a vital opportunity to put people and inclusion back at the center of our agenda. And as a woman myself, to the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action and to the Women, Peace and Security Agenda, including as a candidate to the Security Council for 2027-2028. In short, you can count with Portugal as a steady and reliable partner committed to multilateralism. Thank you.
Thank you. I thank Her Excellency, Minister of Portugal, and now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Tuvalu on behalf of Pacific Small Island Developing States.

Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies, and distinguished delegates. This HLPF's focus on science and evidence-based solutions is timely and appropriate. For Pacific SIDS, science tells us unequivocally that climate change undermines all our development climate, making every challenge more urgent and complex. With SDGs severely off track, the 1.5°C Paris Agreement threshold at risk, and multilateralism under attack, we are confronting a global climate and development emergency. The window for decisive, meaningful action is closing, and closing fast. On health and well-being, Pacific states face critical medical workforce shortages that leave rural communities dangerously underserved. COVID-19 exposed the fragility of our health systems, while climate-induced heat waves intensify existing health vulnerabilities. We are working to address these challenges by increasing health sector investments, but regional medical training partnerships and shared specialized services, together with climate-resilient development, can solve this if supported at scale. Gender equality remains elusive as women continue to face systemic exclusion from economic opportunities. We are making strides with women entering leadership positions and improving gender parity in education, but structural structural barriers continue to persist. Addressing this requires targeted financing to ensure the inclusion of women in key economic sectors and leadership roles. To accelerate economic growth, Pacific SIDS are working to reduce aid dependency and broaden economic opportunities through infrastructure development and targeted social sector investments. But to truly translate these investments into sustained growth, we must boost productivity, and that starts with investing in our people, creating decent and meaningful jobs, and ensuring safe and secure working environments for all. As big ocean states, the ocean defines our identity and economy, yet environmental degradation threatens fisheries and tourism and sea level rise threatens to engulf our lands and livelihoods. The Ocean Conference made commitments, but we must accelerate their implementation, including by boosting investment in ocean science, technology transfer, and marine research infrastructure. If we are to truly achieve the SDGs, we must address these systemic challenges now with transformational action. We urgently need the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index operationalized with binding commitments from international financial institutions and the immediate operationalization of the Loss and Damage Fund with substantial predictable funding streams. Excellencies, we commend our fellow P6 members, the Federated States of Micronesia and Papua New Guinea, on the presentation of their VNRS at this forum. Their comprehensive reports demonstrate both the progress achieved and challenges that persist across our region. Pacific SIDS are showing leadership by boosting public investment in health and education while deepening partnerships with civil society. What we need are partners who match our urgency with their resources our innovation with their investments, and our determination with their political will. In 5 years, we will either celebrate success together or explain our collective failure to the next generation. Let this HLBF be the turning point, a moment of collective resolve to put the SDGs back on track. Mr. President, I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Tuvalu on behalf of Pacific seats, and now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malawi.

Malawi acknowledges the critical role of this year's focus on SDG 3, 5, 8, 14, and 17 as they represent key enablers of a resilient, inclusive, and sustainable development pathway. We have made some progress. For instance, SDG 5, gender equality. Malawi continues to make progress in advancing gender equality, introducing reduction in child marriages from 47% to 44% in 2020 and 2023. The government remains firmly committed to strengthening the legal protections expanding opportunities for women's economic empowerment, and promoting transformative social norms that uphold the rights and dignity of women. On SDG 8, Decent Work and Economic Growth, Malawi is advancing inclusive and sustainable economic growth through targeted reforms that promote job creation, resilience, and structural transformation. We are diversifying the economy by investing in agro- industrialization, mining, and manufacturing, with a strong focus on empowering youth through skills development and entrepreneurship. On SDG 17, Partnership for SDGs, Malawi has increased domestic revenue mobilization from 11.8% to 14.1% of GDP, with a target of 17.1% this year. In addition, Malawi has developed SDG Investor Map to solicit private sector participation in public sector investments. We recognize that public sources alone are not adequate to achieve the attainment of SDG by 2030. This affirms our resolve towards fiscal self-reliance through international partnership that remain indispensable. Mr. President, recognizing the slow pace in some areas, we are undertaking a midterm review to evaluate our implementation strategies We are developing an acceleration plan to close gaps and fast-track delivery in our SDG targets. Infrastructure and energy development remains our fundamental enablers. We are expanding our energy generation capacity, more investment in roads and other transport infrastructure, and undertaking policy reforms to stimulate trade, private investment, and industrialization. In closing, Mr. President, We call for increased concessional financing, technology transfer, capacity building, and fair trade to support structural transformation. We urge development partners to honour ODA commitments and align support with national priorities grounded in mutual accountability and respect for national ownership. I thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malawi. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Qatar.

Your Excellency, President of the ECOSOC, your distinguished members of the Bureau, thank you for leading this forum. I would like to thank the Secretariat of the United Nations out of appreciation for their efforts to organize this forum and to provide sustainable solutions in support of the SDGs and to guarantee that no one is left behind. As we draw closer to the 80th anniversary of the UN, Qatar reiterates its commitment to the fundamental principles of the Agenda 2030. Our commitment is based on our national commitment through the Qatar Vision 2030. Which is ambitious and that is based on a solid will to achieve the goals. Your Excellencies, the State of Qatar believes firmly that sustainable development cannot be achieved by any country alone. It is a journey that requires collaboration, and accordingly, the State of Qatar continues to expand to expand its cooperation with the United Nations and its agencies. We are proud with our partnership in Doha, and we have excellent partnerships with UNDP and UNEP and UNICEF and different agencies in support of international efforts and out of solidarity. And while we look towards the future, the journey towards sustainable development. We embark on the journey from solid ground, and we engage in cooperation out of a sense of shared responsibility. And we would like to present some of our achievements. We have provided assistance in the value of $600 million in one year, and we have— Please, We have achieved paradigm shifts in the energy sector in our country, accelerating the pace towards our clean energy goals, and we are reinforcing our social protection systems. The road to 2030 is not only through strategies, but it requires serious political will and collaboration on all levels. We'll continue to cooperate with all partners to achieve our desired goals for the benefit of the present and future generations. And thank you for your attention.
I thank the distinguished representative of Qatar. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Italy.

Distinguished presidents, Distinguished delegates, it is an honor to address this forum and reaffirm Italy's commitment to the 2030 Agenda by describing our 4 main areas of work. First, the implementation of the 2030 Agenda is a national responsibility, one that must be anchored in a long-term vision, supported through an inclusive dialogue, and grounded in actions at every level of governance. Our National Sustainable Development Strategy represents our roadmap, and we are committed to delivering on it. Second, sustainable development will not be achieved if fragment efforts are set in place. Strengthening policy coherence is essential to prevent conflicting outcomes and to ensure that progress in one area does not come at the expense of another. So we developed a national action plan to ensure alignment across ministries, policies, and with local authorities. And thirdly, no single actor can achieve the SDGs alone. Our National Forum on Sustainable Development plays a critical role in ensuring meaningful participatory processes, enhancing collaboration and extensive dialogue with civil society, academia, private sector actors, youth organizations, and local authorities. Fourth, progress on SDGs depends on our ability to apply them in everyday life. Italy supports local authorities in integrating SDGs in local strategies and policies and aligning them with national strategic objectives. It is in this spirit that the— with UN-Habitat, we launched the Partnership Platform on Localizing the SDGs at the HLPF this year with 12 countries and will formalize their participation. We will celebrate collaboration partner countries also with the integration of sports through strengthened collaboration with the International Olympic Committee. In concluding, distinguished President, Italy is ensuring a multinational, multidimensional support to global partners, with a special focus on Africa through the implementation of the Mattei Plan, and with small island states and other countries in vulnerable situations. At UNOC 3, Italy presented 13 voluntary commitments aimed at the protection and sustainable use of ocean and seas for a total amount of €115 million. with a particular focus on the challenges faced by youth in Small Island Developing States, as well as to the needs of the Mediterranean Sea. Finally, Honourable President, next year Italy will be presenting its 3rd VNR with the aim to share our efforts, further strengthen our collective actions, and contribute to building a future that is better for all while leaving no one behind. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Italy. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Poland.

Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. The main topic of today's debate is a clear and robust call to action. No other ways. The world stands at a historical crossroads. On the one hand, we face complex challenges. Climate crisis, deepening inequalities, and geopolitical instability. On the other, we are presented with unique opportunities fueled by the developments in science, technology, and international cooperation. We hope that UNAT initiative will create a new momentum for global transformation to consolidate achievements made so far and accelerate sustained development worldwide. Today, the international community requires renewed energy and strengthened trust in multilateral institutions. The UN 80 process offers a vital space to streamline constructive dialogue on the reform of the United Nations system. Poland firmly believes that the UNAIDS initiative should reinforce the fundamental values and goals of the United Nations, in particular this articulated in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Pact for the Future. We stress the importance of providing member states with detailed and timely information on planned action their rational financial implication, and monitoring the implementation of initiative. Equally important is the involvement of UN entities and regional hubs beyond New York in shaping and executing these efforts. Any reform should aim to increase effectiveness and tangible outcomes on the ground. In this regard, supporting the implementation of the 2030 Agenda remains paramount. UNAIDS offers a critical opportunity to remodel global partnership anchored in evidence, scientific knowledge, and innovation, but equally grounded in solidarity and shared responsibility. Poland remains a committed partner in efforts to strengthen the UN system as an active member state and a constructive contributor to global peace, human rights, and sustainable development. We believe the UN80 can serve as a turning point, catalyst for meaningful reform, and driver of a more just secure and sustainable future for all. Thank you, delegates. Thank you, President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Polska, and now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Equatorial Guinea.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. It is an honor to address this high-level political forum representing the National Council for Economic and Social Development of Equatorial Guinea, a constitutional advisory technical body of the state on economic and social policy that was recently established. After its first year of operation, it has begun to lay the groundwork for more inclusive, technical, and coherent participation in processes for the planning and follow-up of sustainable development in our country. In this brief institutional history, we have prioritized the establishment of a permanent dialogue with all economic and social actors in the nation as a way to strengthen national ownership of the Sustainable Development Goals while leaving no one behind. We have begun processes of technical advisory services for public policies, particularly in key areas such as economic diversification, youth employability, and environmental sustainability, which are subjects of concern and a top priority on the political and economic agenda of our presidency. Equatorial Guinea reaffirms its commitment to the Sustainable Development Goals, and the National Council for Economic and Social Development is supporting this process through rigorous analysis, multi-sectoral dialogue, and proposals that prioritize equity, sustainability, and the well-being of our population. We recognize that the challenges are great. But so is our determination. We call for strengthened international cooperation, sustainable financing, and the exchange of good practices. We reiterate our commitment to the 2030 Agenda, and we welcome the opportunity to share this space, which inspires and incentivizes young institutions such as ours to become key actors in the construction of equitable, resilient, and people-centered development. In Equatorial Guinea, we will continue to work so that the 2030 Agenda can be a living and effective guide for the transformation of our societies. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Equatorial Guinea, and now I give the floor To the distinguished representative of Mali.

Mr. President, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I would like to begin by conveying the cordial and fraternal greetings of the people of Mali, led by His Excellency General Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition and Head of State. Mali, like many other developing nations, has always shown keen interest in participating in this high-level meeting to reaffirm its full commitment to contributing to the achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. In this regard, Mali fully supports the theme of this forum, Advancing Lasting, Inclusive, Science-Based Sustainable Development Solutions. towards 2030 and the SDGs to leave no one behind, and welcomes the relevance of the SDGs selected for review. President, ladies and gentlemen, following the Summit of the Future held in September 2024, which laid the foundation for a fresh start toward achieving the SDGs, it is essential for nations to take innovative initiatives to address the crises facing our world. My country, Mali, located in the heart of the Sahel, has faced enormous challenges and obstacles to its development for decades, including climate change, its landlocked geography, and the effects of a multidimensional security crisis fueled by terrorist groups and their foreign state sponsors. To break this vicious cycle once and for all, the Government of Mali, under the leadership of General Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition and head of state, is implementing significant reforms to rebuild the state. In the short term, the government's action plan for 2025-26 focuses on 8 priority areas, which stem from recommendations made during major national consultations, including the National Refoundation Conferences, the Inter-Malian Dialogue, and strategic framework documents such as the 2063 Mali Koura Vision and the National Strategy for Emergence. Thank you. And sustainable development for 2024-2033, with a total cost of 61 billion CFA francs, or approximately $110 billion. The National Sustainable Development Strategy requires increased resource mobilization efforts. This effort will be primarily national. Indeed, in line with the head of state's vision, Mali is committed to a national ownership approach to development by mobilizing domestic resources. This includes broadening the tax base, controlling mining and land transactions, as well as better organization of contributions from the diaspora. At the regional level, the Confederation of Sahel States, which brings together Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, was established in July 2024 to accelerate sustainable development for the benefit of our populations, ensuring no one is left behind. To this end, the Alliance of Sahel States is working to pool the efforts of the 3 countries to eradicate poverty.
And I thank the High Representative of Mali. And now I give the floor to the High Representative of Cyprus.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished guests, it's my honour to address the High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development Republic of Cyprus aligns itself with the statement of the European Union and welcomes this opportunity to reaffirm our commitment to the 2030 Agenda and its promise to leave no one behind. As a small state in the Eastern Mediterranean, Cyprus experiences firsthand the challenges and opportunities of sustainable development, from bridging the gender gap in leadership to addressing marine pollution to building an inclusive green and blue economy. And as a current member of the Human Rights Council, Cypres approaches the SDGs through a rights-based lens, with people and planet at the center of our national and international action. Cypres believes that gender equality is a core foundation, not a footnote of sustainable development. We are prioritizing women's leadership in climate resilience, education, and digital transformation, ensuring that girls and young women have the tools, support, and freedoms to shape their own futures. We condemn all forms of sex— of gender-based violence and remain fully committed to advancing sexual and reproductive health and rights as an essential component of SDG 3 and broader human rights obligations. As an island state, the sea is not just our geography. It is our identity, our economy, and our responsibility. Cyprus reiterates its unwavering support for the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea which remains the only comprehensive legal framework governing all maritime affairs. We strongly support the timely and inclusive implementation of the BBNJ agreement and call for the enhanced investment in marine conservation, data sharing, and regional cooperation in the Mediterranean Sea. Combating plastic pollution, protecting biodiversity, and empowering coastal communities, including promoting women in the maritime sector, fisheries and marine science are national and regional priorities. Mr. President, true multilateralism is built on the respect of the Charter, equity, solidarity, and shared responsibility. Cyprus supports stronger engagement between and with all member states, especially through capacity building, technology transfer, and inclusive financing mechanisms that leave no one behind. We also acknowledge the multiple interconnected challenges confronting the least developed countries and landlocked developing countries, including increased vulnerability to external shocks. Having been a committed member of the Small Island Developing States, Cyprus remains deeply aware of the unique vulnerabilities faced by small climate-sensitive economies. These challenges are far from theoretical. They represent tangible and ongoing barriers to achieving sustainable development. Addressing them demands focused inclusive and sustained international cooperation and support. The COVID-19 pandemic reaffirmed the importance of resilient, inclusive health systems. Cyprus is expanding universal access to quality healthcare, with particular focus on mental health.

Thank you. I believe the time is up. Please submit the full version of your statement to the Secretariat. I thank the distinguished representative of Cyprus. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mauritania.

Mr. President, President of ECOSOC, ladies and gentlemen, Excellencies, we thank you most sincerely for the organization of this High-Level Forum. The Islamic Republic of Mauritania reaffirms its steadfast commitment to the implementation of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda and its 17 goals through ambitious national policies that are people-centered and in line with our capacities. In this context, The Strategy for Accelerated Growth and Shared Prosperity, or SCAP, serves as the comprehensive framework for accelerating economic growth while ensuring fair distribution of its dividends through the promotion of social justice, reducing poverty, and fostering inclusion. One of the key tools for the implementation of this strategy is the National Agency for Solidarity, which implements major social programs for vulnerable groups. This includes cash transfers, health insurance, and support for small businesses while expanding access to essential services and remote services. To date, this The strategy is also reviewing its contribution to the BBNJ. We are also reviewing our nationally determined contribution under the Paris Agreement. The country is implementing a 5-year plan for the environment and for development in order to fight climate change, desertification, and to preserve biodiversity. Our country is actively participating in international negotiations on plastic pollution, biodiversity, desertification, as we are aware of our environmental situation. In conclusion, the Government of Mauritania remains committed to achieving the SDGs based on clear national strategies and through socioeconomic and environmental approaches involving strong international partnerships in order to build a better future for everyone. Thank you.
Representative of Mauritania. And now I give the floor to this distinguished representative of Bahrain.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, it is an honor to address this year's High-Level Political Forum as the UN celebrates its 80th anniversary. A moment for reflection and renewal. Guided by the vision of His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa and the directives of His Royal Highness Prince Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, Bahrain continues to reaffirm its commitment to the 2030 Agenda and to sustained global cooperation, especially at a time when momentum must be catalyzed and expanded through partnership, innovation, and shared ambition. Our Economic Vision 2030, centered around sustainability, competitiveness, and fairness, helped us shape the wave of transformation witnessed today by laying a clear path for progress. This roadmap contributed to a clear shift from an oil-based economy to a diversified and globally competitive one. With non-oil sectors now contributing to approximately 86% of GDP, which serves as a testament to the success of our policies. Bahrain's financial services sector, now the largest GDP contributor, serves as a key driver for growth and innovation. Our inclusive financial system has helped position the Kingdom as a pioneer in digital financial infrastructure innovation by expanding mobile payments, strengthening regulations, prioritizing financial integrity and stability, and promoting digitization and financial innovation. Our fintech ecosystem has also broadened access to finance, especially for SMEs, women, and youth-led enterprises. Through our labor fund, Temkeen, we are future-proofing our workforce with plans to train 50,000 Bahrainis in AI by 2030. This commitment to science and evidence-based progress also shapes our approach to healthcare. Bahrain's strong healthcare system has enabled us to adopt groundbreaking science-based technologies such as the National Genome Project, launched in 2019, which advances personalized medicine by mapping the kingdom's genetic profile to prevent hereditary diseases, enhance early detection, and improve long-term well-being. Additionally, in 2025, Bahrain achieved a critical medical milestone by successfully treating a sickle cell patient using the Casgevy technology, a CRISPR-based gene editing therapy which reflects how data-driven innovation is transforming our health system to become more innovative, predictive, inclusive, and resilient. Chairperson, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, Zambia aligns itself with the statement delivered by the Group of 77 and China. As we commemorate the 80th anniversary of the United Nations, this occasion serves not only as a moment for reflection but as a critical opportunity to stimulate transformative action in pursuit of the 2030 Agenda. With just 5 years before 2030, it is evident that SDGs remain severely off track. The Pact for the Future is a foundational framework to realign international cooperation for sustainable development. Mr. President, I have the honor to deliver the following statement on behalf of the Alliance of Small Island States, AOSIS. This year's Forum comes at a crucial juncture. With just 5 years left to deliver on the promise of the 2030 Agenda, the message is clear: the world is not on track. Cities are living the consequences of eroding multilateralism and global inaction— rising sea levels, worsening climate disasters, and escalating debt burdens. The climate crisis is no longer a distant threat. It is a daily reality that impacts our lives and livelihoods. Our progress on the SDGs has been slow and uneven, often undermined by external shocks beyond our control. We are often the first to be hit and the last to recover. Therefore, we call on the international community to uphold the principle that SIDS are a special case for sustainable development, as recognized in the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, the 2030 Agenda and boldly reasserted in the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for States, ABAS. The ABAS reflects the unique circumstances of small islands and charts a course that integrates climate action, economic resilience, and sustainable development. But its implementation cannot wait. We urge all partners to match the political will of the ABAS with financial, technical, and institutional support necessary to bring its ambition to life. The HLPF must be a catalyst for delivery. We welcome the Sevilla Commitment adopted at F54 as a concrete step forward. Its call for reforming the global financial architecture, starting with the full operationalization and the use of the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index, must be acted upon. The MDI reflects a fundamental truth: GDP per capita cannot capture the real risks and vulnerabilities that SIDS face. The Debt Sustainability Support Service, DSSS, is another critical initiative whose operationalization must be accelerated. With so many SIDS grappling with unsustainable debt burdens, the DSSS represents an important tool to unlock fiscal space while supporting long-term resilience. We also call for the full support of the SIDS a center of excellence. This institution will empower SIDS to lead with our own expertise, data, and innovation that are fit for our realities and rooted in our priorities. Lastly, we firmly reject the imposition of unilateral coercive economic measures that are inconsistent with the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and international law. We call on the international community to eliminate the use of such measures. Mr. President, we cannot speak of our sustainable development without speaking of the ocean. This year's review of SDG 14 has reaffirmed that the ocean is our foundation. It sustains our economies, nourishes our communities, and anchors our identities, yet it remains the least, least funded SDG. From the commitments made at the 3rd United Nations Ocean Conference in Nice to the historic decisions by ITLOS and at COP28, We are seeing a growing recognition that ocean health is inextricably linked to climate change, sustainable development, and biodiversity, but we must move from recognition to action. This means significantly scaling up investment in marine protection, sustainable fisheries, ocean-based economies, and technologies that can help us monitor and protect vast ocean spaces. Mr. President, AOSIS remains steadfast in our resolve. We are doing our part with limited means and infinite will, but we cannot do it alone. We urge this forum to treat the development of small island states not as peripheral to the global agenda, but central to it. If we fail SIDS, we fail the 2030 Agenda. But if we enable SIDS to thrive, we unlock solutions that can benefit the entire world. The time to act is now. The tools are within our reach. Let us deliver. I thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President. This is a joint statement on behalf of the Pathfinders for Peaceful, Just and Inclusive Societies. It was co-facilitated by the Permanent Missions of Colombia and the Republic of Korea, and a complete version will be shared with the Secretariat to be uploaded. Distinguished delegates, the world is at an inflection point. We are living through a period of disruption characterized by compounding crises, megatrends, intensifying geopolitical tensions, inequality, and war. Multilateralism and the credibility of global institutions are under extraordinary strain. Official assistance is failing, and the frameworks that once unified international action, including the SDGs, are being questioned as the UN undergoes major reforms. Governance at all levels is stressed, testing its capacity to respond, adapt and deliver for people and planet. At the same time, democracy itself faces growing threats, and the rise of political extremism exploits social divides and undermines trust in institutions. The question is not if we are at a turning point, but how we will respond. Despite challenges, we know that progress on the SDGs is possible. And that peace, justice, equality and inclusion are not just aspirational but possible, with links and dividends across development, economic and security priorities, including as related to this year's SDGs under review. Violence is a public health issue, with far-reaching effects on physical and mental well-being. To this end, there is a 14-year life expectancy gap between the most and least violent countries. Similarly, 29% of people suffer health problems due to poor access to justice. Conversely, inclusive institutions are key to public health, and tackling the root causes of inequality through a social determinants of health approach is key to advancing the SDGs and building more resilient and healthier societies. More equal societies also have better growth rates, benefiting not only the most vulnerable but all members of society. On this, investing in healthcare, housing and women's access to labour markets can unlock significant and inclusive economic growth. Closing the gender gap could give the global economy a $7 trillion boost. Similarly, equitable justice systems foster gender equality and gender-equal societies support a stronger rule of law. Countries with gender-equal legal codes score higher on access to justice rankings, with women's access to decision-making correlated with lower levels of gender-based violence. And on oceans, inclusion, accountability, and anti-corruption enhance marine and coastal protection, promote fishery sustainability, and support climate adaptation and resilience. Improved women's representation in ocean-related decision-making, strengthens community livelihoods, and supports a sustainable blue economy. But peace, justice, equality, and inclusion not only enable broader development priorities; they are also cost-effective, critical in today's landscape. Targeted investments in violence prevention and access to justice can deliver hard economic returns several times the initial outlay. Governance and institutions are key, to de-risking private and public investment and attracting the necessary capital. The SDGs are badly off track and there are no silver bullets. Yet peace, justice, equality and inclusion offer actionable approaches to and solutions for progress across the SDGs and a means to rebuild trust in institutions and governance. Behind every statistic are people and communities who are struggling and who deserve to live lives free from fear, insecurity, and injustice. As we face rising threats to democratic norms and an alarming resurgence of far-right extremism in many regions, our commitment to democratic values, human rights, and pluralism must remain unwavering. We must be inclusive, involving all stakeholders and especially civil society if we want to continue to bring this from global to local. Cross-regional coalitions like the Pathfinders are examples of inclusive and effective multilateralism. Going forward, we must bridge divides and strengthen solidarity by investing in people to realize their full potential, investing in institutions to deliver fairly, and investing in systems to uphold cohesion and a social contract grounded in peace, justice, inclusion, and equitable governance. I thank you, Mr. President.

It is our obligation to strengthen global health systems, invest in prevention, and ensure the health equality equity and social participation become central elements of health systems. The obligation to protect human rights extends to gender equality. 5 years to 2030, the progress remains uneven and insufficient. Women are still affected by gender-based violence and discrimination. It is sinister that nearly 1 in 4 countries is seeing a backlash against women's rights. There can be no sustainable development without equality for all women and girls. We must renew our commitment to a world where equal rights and opportunities are not an exception, but the norm. And the UN should lead the way. Slovenia strongly supports efforts to achieve gender parity in the UN system, including in highest decision-making positions. So, ladies and gentlemen, sustainable development is not a catchphrase, but the only viable path to survival. We have to—

Thank you. That was a crucial last sentence, no, about the survival. Thank you. I thank the distinguished Permanent Representative of Slovenia. And now I give the floor to the Permanent Representative of South Africa.

Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. As we celebrate the UN at 80, South Africa reaffirms its deep commitment to multilateralism, to the principles of the UN Charter, and to the 2030 Agenda and Sustainable Development Goals. We must not forget that sustainable development is a daily imperative for millions across the Global South as the legacy of colonialism, persistent structural inequalities, and environmental vulnerabilities continue to shape our development realities. We join the global call to action for transformative change for sustainable development. As the current G20 President, we are encouraging a paradigm shift to accelerate the implementation of the practical solutions to achieve the 2030 Agenda and its SDGs. South Africa's theme of solidarity, equality, sustainability addresses the core of the original G20 mandate of promoting strong, sustainable, balanced, and inclusive growth, leaving no one behind. In the national context, Our National Development Plan is strongly aligned with the SDGs and the African Union Agenda 2063. We have made considerable progress, and yet the triple challenges of unemployment, poverty, inequality remain pressing, especially amongst youth. We are committed to contextualizing the SDGs at the local level. Mr. President, as the global context continues to evolve, the UN must evolve to remain fit for purpose. South Africa strongly supports reform of the UN system, including the Security Council. We further call on the UN system to intensify efforts to support technology transfer, digital inclusion, and capacity development to address the digital divide. South Africa supports the UN80 initiative approach that addresses the 3 areas of engagement of inefficiencies, mandate review, and structural changes, and in so doing, the core mandate of the UN as espoused within our Charter. And that Charter should remain the guiding beacon. An improved UN system is a fundamental requirement for maintaining an effective multilateral governance framework resulting in concrete outcomes for advancing global peace and security. sustainable inclusive growth and development, and promoting human rights. Let us mark this 80th anniversary not only with remembrance, but with resolve to catalyze change, build resilience, and deliver a sustainable future for all. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished Permanent Representative of South Africa. Now I give the floor to the distinguished Permanent Representative of Türkiye.

Thank you, Mr. President. 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development remains our collective roadmap, and Türkiye is a staunch supporter. To turn this vision into reality, we must directly confront the structural constraints that have long hindered progress in developing and least developed countries. We note with deep concern that the SDG investment gap in developing countries now exceeds $4 trillion annually. Despite some setbacks, we cannot relent in our resolve and determination to do our utmost to rescue the SDGs. Türkiye welcomes recent development of the Sevilla Outcome Document. There are a number of upcoming occasions to drive implementation. The World Summit for Social Development The SDG Summit and the review of the Global Digital Compact, as well as the review of the Pact for Future in 2028, are some of the most prominent opportunities. Strong ownership and leadership by governments is a must for the timely implementation of the SDGs. Yet, stronger partnerships with local authorities, private sector, civil society and academia can have a real impact. We have taken a holistic approach to SDG action by integrating them into the national development plans and sectoral strategies. Our 12th National Development Plan is grounded on Sustainable Development Agenda. Turkey is leading the way for circular economy by promoting zero waste initiatives as a game changer for sustainable development. We are also leveraging our financial resources, expertise, and partnerships to contribute to global efforts to achieve SDGs. Türkiye has become a prominent actor in international development cooperation. It is based on non-interference in internal affairs, mutual respect, no conditionality, respect for sovereignty, and mutual benefit. At an era where digital transformation has become key to unlocking sustainable development, We have been supporting LDCs through UN Technology Bank in Istanbul for the structural transformation. As a country that serves as a bridge between the developed and developing world, we are uniquely positioned to play an inclusive and mobilizing role by hosting COP 31 with your support in Türkiye in 2026. Türkiye, already hosting numerous UN offices in both Ankara and Istanbul, stands ready to contribute actively and constructively to the reform process. Thanks for the attention.

I thank the distinguished Permanent Representative of Türkiye. Thank you, Mr. President. We deny the libelous accusations by the Palestinian delegation that only serve as an attempt to vilify our country, which is defending itself against the terrorist threat of Hamas and other terrorist groups. We regret that the Palestinian representative did not find it appropriate to condemn the control of a terror organization over the Palestinian people in Gaza, and which still holds 50 Israeli hostages. While we firmly reject any false or politically motivated accusations, Israel welcomes an honest debate. As a liberal democracy, we do not shy away from criticism. That said, we believe that any attempt to politicize this conversation does a disservice to the core purpose of our gathering. It is particularly troubling when such interventions overlook the very real and relevant tragedy of what happens when radical elements actively neglect sustainable development and instead invest in furthering extremism and division. Let me conclude by reaffirming that Israel stands ready to work with all who are genuinely committed to improving the lives of their people through innovation, cooperation, and a shared sense of purpose. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of Israel, and now I give the floor to the representative of Russian Federation.

Thank you, Mr. President. We must exercise the right of reply in connection with the statement delivered by Latvia. We call on all countries to refrain from aggressive rhetoric and accusations and to use this forum for constructive dialogue on development issues. Thank you.
